You reason through contraindications: triptans and ergots (dihydroergotamine) are vasoconstrictors and contraindicated in CAD; NSAIDs like naproxen are risky in renal insufficiency; opioids are inappropriate for routine migraine abortion. That leaves a CGRP antagonist, rimegepant, which lacks vasoconstrictive activity and is suitable here. The resident learns to screen every migraine abortive against cardiac and renal status before prescribing. Bottom line: In migraine with cardiovascular disease, skip triptans and ergots and reach for a gepant like rimegepant.

stem: A 35-year-old is seen by a chiropractor for treatment of mild neck discomfort. The patient undergoes manipulation of the neck and shortly after develops dysarthric speech, gait ataxia, and numbness over the right body. In addition, the patient complains of increased severity of neck pain radiating to the occiput. The likely etiology of this patient's symptoms is:
scenario: A 35-year-old comes to the ED minutes after chiropractic neck manipulation with dysarthria, gait ataxia, right-sided numbness, and severe neck pain radiating to the occiput. You connect the mechanical neck trauma to a posterior-circulation syndrome and suspect vertebral artery dissection causing brainstem or cerebellar ischemia. This drives immediate stroke-protocol activation, CT or MR angiography of the neck vessels, and neurology and vascular consultation rather than treating it as benign musculoskeletal pain or migraine. Bottom line: Brainstem-cerebellar signs with neck pain after neck manipulation mean vertebral artery dissection until proven otherwise, so image the vessels urgently.

stem: The consultation-liaison psychiatrist evaluates a 54-year-old patient with end-stage breast cancer. The patient was previously very optimistic and energetic but has recently been told that the treatment protocol had failed and only palliative care was recommended. Since that time the patient has appeared depressed, and the team is concerned that she is suicidal. On interview, the patient is initially pleasant and able to amiably discuss neutral topics. When the subject shifts to her illness, the patient becomes tearful and expresses a crushing feeling of hopelessness about the future. She denies any plan to hurt herself, saying, "What's the point? I'm going to die soon anyway, but I would rather God just took me and didn't draw this out." Which of the following would be the best initial approach to this patient?
scenario: As the C-L psychiatrist you see a 54-year-old with end-stage breast cancer who became tearful and hopeless after learning treatment failed; the team fears she is suicidal. On interview she denies any plan and says she wishes God would simply take her without prolonging things, a passive wish reflecting demoralization rather than major depression or active suicidality. Your best first move is to validate her grief as a normal, expectable response to an overwhelming loss, building alliance before assessing whether a treatable depressive syndrome is also present. You avoid a knee-jerk locked-unit transfer or premature medication. Bottom line: Demoralization at end of life calls first for empathic validation, not reflexive hospitalization or diagnosis of major depression.

stem: A 75-year-old patient presents with progressive gait Imbalance, recurrent falls, and cognitive decline over the last several years. A computed tomography scan of the brain is shown below. Which of the following interventions is most likely to slow further progression of the disease process?
scenario: A 75-year-old is referred to your geriatric clinic for cognitive decline, and the family is also describing a magnetic, shuffling gait and new urinary incontinence, with recurrent falls. CT shows enlarged ventricles out of proportion to atrophy. You recognize the triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus, gait, cognition, urinary, and crucially, this dementia is potentially reversible. Instead of just starting a cholinesterase inhibitor, you refer for a large-volume lumbar puncture (tap test) and neurosurgical evaluation for a CSF ventriculoperitoneal shunt, which can slow or reverse progression. Bottom line: The NPH triad warrants a tap test and CSF shunt, treatable dementia.

stem: A 50-year-old patient has a bilateral hand tremor, which worsens with arm extension and eating. It improves at rest and after drinking alcohol. These features are characteristic of which of the following types of tremor?
scenario: A 50-year-old asks you about a hand tremor that makes soup and coffee a mess. On exam it appears with arm extension and during action like eating, eases at rest, and notably calms after a glass of wine. That pattern, often with a family history, points to essential tremor rather than Parkinson's, whose tremor is present at rest. The alcohol responsiveness and postural-kinetic quality are the giveaway, and they steer treatment toward propranolol or primidone rather than dopaminergic agents. You also caution against self-treating with alcohol. Distinguishing the two prevents a misdiagnosis and the wrong prescription. Bottom line: An action and postural tremor that improves with alcohol and at rest is essential tremor; treat with propranolol or primidone.

stem: Which of the following is the leading cause of death in persons with severe mental illness?
scenario: On your community psychiatry rotation you see a 48-year-old with schizophrenia on olanzapine: BMI 38, A1c 8.1, smoker, never had a lipid panel. It's easy to fixate on suicide risk and forget that people with severe mental illness die 15-20 years early, mostly from cardiovascular disease. That fact should reshape your visit. You order metabolic labs, start a statin and metformin conversation, refer to smoking cessation, and reconsider the metabolically harsh antipsychotic. Psychiatrists are often these patients' only medical contact, so monitoring weight, glucose, lipids, and blood pressure is your job, not just the PCP's. Bottom line: Cardiovascular disease, not suicide, kills most people with severe mental illness, so screen and treat metabolic risk aggressively.

stem: Which of the following can be a normal neurological exam finding in older adults?
scenario: An 80-year-old comes to clinic worried she's developing neuropathy because her feet feel 'less buzzy.' On exam you find absent vibratory sense at the great toes but intact proprioception, normal strength, symmetric reflexes, and no sensory level. Knowing that diminished distal vibratory sensation is an expected aging change, you avoid an unnecessary alarm and a costly workup, while still documenting that the rest of the exam is reassuringly normal. You counsel her on fall prevention and footwear instead. Contrast this with ankle clonus, a sensory level, or asymmetric weakness, which are never normal and demand investigation. Bottom line: isolated loss of vibration at the toes is a normal finding in older adults, not automatic evidence of disease.

stem: Vindictiveness and arguing with authority figures are important characteristics of which of the following childhood disorders?
scenario: In your child clinic, parents bring an 8-year-old who is 'always fighting.' You probe the pattern: he loses his temper, deliberately annoys siblings, blames others, and is spiteful and vindictive, but he does not steal, harm animals, or violate others' basic rights. That distinction matters. Recognizing the angry, argumentative, vindictive triad as oppositional defiant disorder rather than conduct disorder steers you toward parent management training and away from a harsher prognosis. You screen for comorbid ADHD and mood symptoms, which frequently co-travel. Documenting the absence of rights-violating behavior also protects the child from a premature conduct disorder label. Bottom line: vindictiveness plus arguing with authority defines ODD, distinguishing it from the rights-violating behavior of conduct disorder.

stem: A 72-year-old patient with two days of confusion and fever Is evaluated in the emergency department for new-onset seizure. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain demonstrates hemorrhage and swelling In the temporal lobes. Cerebrospinal fluid shows increased lymphocytes and protein. Which of the following medications is most likely to be effective in treating the patient's condition?
scenario: The ED calls you about a 72-year-old with two days of fever, confusion, a new seizure, and MRI showing hemorrhagic temporal lobe involvement with a lymphocytic, high-protein CSF. You immediately recognize the signature of herpes simplex encephalitis. The teaching point you act on: do not wait for PCR confirmation. Empiric IV acyclovir started early dramatically reduces mortality and morbidity, and delay is the main driver of bad outcomes. You ensure acyclovir is hung now, send HSV PCR, and avoid being distracted toward bacterial or fungal coverage as the primary fix. Bottom line: temporal lobe hemorrhage with fever and seizures is HSV encephalitis until proven otherwise, so start acyclovir empirically and immediately.

stem: The psychiatrist is considering prescribing donepezil for an 87-year-old patient. Which of the following medications would most significantly interfere with its efficacy?
scenario: Before starting donepezil for an 87-year-old with Alzheimer's, you reconcile her medication list and notice she takes oxybutynin for urge incontinence. You flag it: oxybutynin is a potent anticholinergic that directly opposes the pro-cholinergic mechanism of a cholinesterase inhibitor, blunting cognitive benefit and worsening confusion. Rather than layering drugs that cancel each other out, you coordinate with her PCP to switch to a non-anticholinergic bladder agent like mirabegron. You also scan for other hidden anticholinergics such as diphenhydramine and certain antispasmodics. This single catch protects both efficacy and cognition. Bottom line: anticholinergics like oxybutynin antagonize donepezil's effect, so deprescribe them before blaming the cholinesterase inhibitor for poor response.

stem: A 19-year-old college student who has "always been overweight" complains that she is unable to lose weight despite exercising for an hour, four times a week, over the last year. She describes college as "very stressful," admitting that she sometimes eats a whole pizza or a gallon of ice cream when feeling overwhelmed; this eating pattern is occurring four or five times a week recently. Afterward, she feels remorseful and vomits. She is concerned that she will always be overweight and plans to increase her exercise to two hours a day, six times a week. Which of the following laboratory findings is most likely?
scenario: A 19-year-old of normal-to-high weight describes recurrent binges several times weekly followed by self-induced vomiting and compensatory over-exercise, with intense body-image distress. You diagnose bulimia nervosa. Anticipating complications, you order labs and explain why elevated serum amylase is the expected finding, reflecting salivary gland stimulation from repeated vomiting. You also check electrolytes for the dangerous hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis purging causes, examine for Russell's sign and dental erosion, and start an SSRI plus CBT. The amylase elevation is a useful objective marker that can corroborate covert purging when a patient minimizes. Bottom line: recurrent purging in bulimia classically elevates serum amylase, a clue that can confirm vomiting and prompts you to monitor electrolytes closely.

stem: Which of the following terms describes the relevance of understanding temperament in working with parent-child relational problems?
scenario: In your child clinic, a mother brings her 3-year-old who screams at every transition. She's exhausted and blames herself, asking if she's a bad parent. Rather than pathologizing the toddler or the mother, you frame the friction as a mismatch between the child's high-intensity, slow-to-warm temperament and the family's fast-paced, change-heavy routine. You teach her about goodness of fit: the same temperament thrives in one environment and struggles in another. Together you build predictable warnings before transitions and lower the daily change load. This reframes guilt into actionable parenting strategy and guides the relational intervention. Bottom line: Goodness of fit explains parent-child friction as a temperament-environment match, not a defect in either party.

stem: Which of the following degenerative disorders is associated with atrophy of the caudate nucleus?
scenario: A 40-year-old with new chorea, irritability, and a father who died of a movement disorder comes to clinic. You order MRI and note caudate nucleus atrophy with boxcar ventricles, classic for Huntington disease, and pursue confirmatory CAG repeat testing with genetic counseling. Recognizing the caudate-atrophy signature shifts your differential away from Parkinson or Alzheimer pathology and changes management toward chorea treatment, psychiatric monitoring for depression and suicide risk, and family planning discussions. The structural clue ties the motor, cognitive, and psychiatric picture together. Bottom line: Caudate nucleus atrophy points to Huntington disease, prompting genetic confirmation and psychiatric risk monitoring.

stem: A 24-year-old female seeks her primary care doctors' advice about breast tenderness, bloating, and mood swings. She reports that this happens "like clockwork" every month, a week prior to menses. During this week, she occasionally misses work. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
scenario: A 24-year-old in your clinic describes breast tenderness, bloating, and mood swings that arrive like clockwork the week before her period and occasionally make her miss work. You have her keep a two-month symptom diary confirming the luteal timing and symptom-free follicular phase. The mix of physical and mild mood symptoms causing some impairment, without the severe affective criteria, fits premenstrual syndrome rather than the more disabling PMDD. You start with lifestyle measures, calcium, and NSAIDs, reserving SSRIs for PMDD-level severity. Distinguishing PMS from PMDD and from premenstrual exacerbation of a mood disorder steers you to proportionate treatment. Bottom line: Cyclical luteal-phase physical and mild mood symptoms with limited impairment indicate premenstrual syndrome, not PMDD.

stem: Although physical health and cognitive function may decline in older age, which of the following aspects of life often increases in older age?
scenario: An 80-year-old in your geriatric clinic has worsening arthritis and mild memory slips yet reports feeling more content and at peace than in midlife. Instead of assuming decline equals misery, you recall that subjective well-being and emotional regulation often increase in older age, a phenomenon described in socioemotional selectivity theory. This reframes your assessment: a sudden drop in well-being or pervasive hopelessness is not normal aging and should prompt a depression workup rather than being dismissed as expected. Knowing that contentment commonly rises helps you separate healthy aging from treatable late-life depression. Bottom line: Sense of well-being often increases with age, so pervasive low mood signals pathology, not normal aging.

stem: In addition to engagement in mental health treatment, which of the following interventions has been demonstrated to lower the risk of completed suicide?
scenario: A 40-year-old man with depression and passive suicidal thoughts is being discharged from your ED. You start an antidepressant and arrange follow-up, but before he leaves you ask specifically about firearms at home. He owns two. You spend ten minutes coaching the family on locking the guns at a relative's house and removing extra medications. That conversation, not the no-harm contract some teams still scribble, is the piece with actual evidence behind reducing completed suicide. Means restriction works because most suicidal crises are brief and impulsive; putting time and distance between intent and a lethal method saves lives. Document the lethal-means counseling you provided. Bottom line: For every at-risk patient, counsel on restricting access to lethal means.

stem: A 17-year patient who experienced childhood adversity has a twin diagnosed with schizophrenia. The patient has been having a decline in school performance and has been isolating over the last six months. During the psychiatric examination, there was no evidence of apparent delusions; however, the patient has been experiencing distressing fleeting auditory hallucinations once a week but exhibits intact reality testing. In which time frame will the patient most likely convert from prodrome presentation to first episode psychosis?
scenario: In your early-psychosis clinic a 17-year-old with childhood adversity and a co-twin with schizophrenia is brought in for declining grades and six months of social withdrawal. He has brief, distressing voices about once weekly but knows they are not real, with no fixed delusions. This is an attenuated psychosis (clinical high-risk) syndrome, and you counsel the family that conversion to frank psychosis, when it happens, is heaviest in the first 1-2 years. That timeline drives your plan: close monitoring, avoiding cannabis, treating the mood and anxiety symptoms, and rapid access if symptoms escalate, rather than reflexively starting an antipsychotic now. Bottom line: Clinical high-risk patients convert to first-episode psychosis mostly within the first two years, so monitor intensively early.

stem: Age-related changes in sexual function in older men include a decrease in:
scenario: A 68-year-old man in your clinic is distressed that his erections are softer and he needs more direct stimulation than in his youth. Before reaching for medication or assuming pathology, you normalize the expected age-related changes: decreased penile rigidity, a longer time to achieve erection and orgasm, and a prolonged refractory period. Knowing the baseline lets you distinguish normal aging from a treatable problem, and prompts you to screen for the things that actually drive ED at his age, vascular disease, diabetes, and medications including SSRIs. Bottom line: In aging men, decreased penile rigidity and slower arousal are normal, so distinguish them from treatable causes before intervening.

stem: The typical physical and developmental features of Fetal Alcohol Syndrome include: (Select three.)
scenario: In your child clinic, a 6-year-old with hyperactivity, learning problems, and a foster placement history is referred. While examining him you deliberately inspect the face: you note microcephaly, a thin vermilion upper lip, and a smooth, poorly developed philtrum. These dysmorphic features, combined with growth restriction and neurodevelopmental impairment, prompt you to ask the agency about prenatal alcohol exposure and pursue a fetal alcohol spectrum evaluation rather than stopping at an ADHD label. Recognizing the triad reframes prognosis, guides school accommodations, and prompts counseling for the birth mother and future pregnancies. Bottom line: Microcephaly, thin upper lip, and a smooth philtrum are the classic facial triad of fetal alcohol syndrome, so look at the face before settling on ADHD alone.

stem: A 26-year-old presents for treatment of major depression. On interview, the patient meets criteria for prior manic episodes. Which of the following medications have the best evidence for monotherapy treatment of this patient's bipolar depression? (Select three.)
scenario: A 26-year-old presents with depression but on careful history meets criteria for past mania, so this is bipolar depression, not unipolar. You resist the reflex to start an SSRI or bupropion, which risk switching and have weak evidence here. Instead you select an agent with proven monotherapy efficacy for the bipolar depressive pole: quetiapine, lurasidone, or olanzapine-fluoxetine combination. You weigh metabolic burden, picking lurasidone for a weight-conscious patient and counseling on quetiapine sedation. This evidence-based choice treats the current episode while respecting mood-cycle risk. Bottom line: Quetiapine, lurasidone, and olanzapine-fluoxetine have the best monotherapy evidence for bipolar depression, so reach for these before antidepressants.

stem: Which of the following neurodevelopmental processes predominantly occurs during adolescence and young adulthood?
scenario: A worried parent in clinic asks why her impulsive 17-year-old 'still acts without thinking.' You explain adolescent brain development: during adolescence and young adulthood the brain undergoes synaptic pruning, eliminating excess connections, alongside continued myelination, while gray matter volume actually decreases. The prefrontal cortex matures last. This neurodevelopmental reality grounds your guidance about expecting improving judgment with age, and it informs how you weigh risk-taking, capacity, and prognosis in adolescent patients. Framing impulsivity as a maturational process rather than a fixed trait shapes both your reassurance and your treatment expectations. Bottom line: Synaptic pruning predominates during adolescence and young adulthood as the brain refines its circuitry.
